::: {.why}
The contradiction you found last night is real: any pure diffusion flattens at short maturities, and the market does not, which is the strongest empirical argument for a discontinuous component.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Say why a diffusion's implied smile flattens as maturity goes to zero and why the market's does not.
- Price an option under a jump-diffusion and show it produces short-dated skew that Heston cannot.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Demonstrate the flattening: price short-dated options under your calibrated Heston at maturities from one year down to one week, and plot the implied skew slope against maturity. It goes to zero. Overlay the market's, which does not.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Add jumps: price under Merton's jump-diffusion, either via QuantLib or by the series representation, and show the short-dated skew survives. Then note the honest limitation, which is that jump parameters are very poorly identified from option prices alone because several combinations fit almost equally well.
:::
:::
